newsitem.title: USA: Clinton chooses Thurman as director of AIDS office.
newsitem.headline: Clinton chooses Thurman as director of AIDS office.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday named Sandra Thurman director of the Office of National AIDS Policy, which coordinates federal policy and programmes to combat the disease.
Thurman, who worked on Clinton's election campaigns in 1992 and 1996, was executive director of AID Atlanta, which provides health and support services to people with HIV and AIDS, from 1988 to 1993.
She has spent the past four years with The Task Force for Child Survival and Development at Atlanta's Carter Centre, focusing on child immunisation and the eradication of polio.
Announcing the appointment at a White House ceremony, Clinton praised Thurman for her work on AIDS, particulary at AID Atlanta, which tripled in size during her tenure.

"Her experience in running a large, community-based organisation makes her especially well-equipped to build the partnerships we need throughout our country, where beating the AIDS epidemic will take this kind of teamwork," Clinton said.

Elizabeth Birch, executive director of the Human Rights Campaign gay interest group, praised Thurman in a statement, saying: "She brings the right mix of leadership, political skills and commitment to the fight against HIV and AIDS."
Others were less pleased, with a spokesman for the ACT UP AIDS group, Wayne Turner, denouncing Thurman as the fourth in a series of "ineffective, no-name bureacrats" in the job.

Some groups have been pressing Clinton to name a more senior official and to upgrade the position to Cabinet status. Thurman will replace Eric Goosby, the office's interim director, who succeeded Patsy Fleming and Kristine Gebbie.
AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by HIV (Human Immuno-deficiency Virus) and attacks the body's immune system. There is no known cure for the disease.
